--- title: "Running scenarios" --- A `Scenario` describes one setting and one campaign, and `run_scenarios` takes a list of them and returns a table with one row each. Both objects are plain dataclasses, importable from either `estimint` or `estimint.scenarios`. We describe the fields a scenario takes, run five of them that between them exercise every input the pipeline accepts, and read the results back. ```python from estimint import run_scenarios from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget ``` ## The seven required fields These have no defaults and must be given for every scenario. Together they describe the setting as it stands, before anything is done to it. | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `name` | A label. It is echoed into the results and is how you index them afterwards. | | `res_use` | Pyrethroid resistance, 0 (fully susceptible) to 1 (fully resistant). | | `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1. | | `phi` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed. Enters the emulator as `phi_bednets`. | | `seasonal` | 0 for perennial transmission, 1 for strongly seasonal. | | `irs` | IRS coverage currently in place. Enters the emulator as `irs_use`. | | `eir_target` | An `EirTarget`. How transmission intensity is specified. | Three of these are renamed on the way in. `phi` becomes `phi_bednets` and `irs` becomes `irs_use`. `res_use` is not a covariate at all, and is consumed by the `dn0` curves without ever reaching the emulator. What the emulator sees is the [twelve static covariates](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd). ## The three input modes `EirTarget(input_value, input_mode)` says what quantity you are handing over. The emulator only ever runs from an EIR, so the mode decides how much work `estimint` has to do first. | Mode | You supply | What happens | |---|---|---| | `"prevalence"` | Under-5 parasite prevalence in [0.005, 0.80] | `estimint` inverts it to an EIR with the XGBoost prevalence model. | | `"eir"` | An EIR, infectious bites per person per year | Used directly. No inversion. | | `"hbr"` | A human biting rate | Converted to an EIR through the HBR model. | Use `"prevalence"` when the evidence is a cross-sectional survey. Use `"eir"` when the EIR is already in hand, or is the quantity being swept over, and `"hbr"` when the evidence is entomological. Note that `mosquito_delta` only applies to `"prevalence"`. Supplied alongside an `"eir"` or an `"hbr"` input it is silently ignored, because there is no prevalence-to-EIR step for it to modify. The mechanism is set out in [Mosquito density and EIR](../04-estimint/mosquito-density.qmd). ## The ten defaulted fields Everything else defaults, and every default is zero or `None`. | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `py_only` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-only nets. | | `py_pbo` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PBO nets. | | `py_pyrrole` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-pyrrole nets. | | `py_ppf` | `0.0` | Current coverage of pyrethroid-PPF nets. | | `mosquito_delta` | `0.0` | Proportional change in mosquito density. Must be > −1. | | `itn_future` | `0.0` | Net coverage from the campaign. | | `net_type_future` | `None` | Net product from the campaign. | | `irs_future` | `0.0` | IRS coverage from the campaign. | | `routine` | `0.0` | Routine (continuous) net distribution from the campaign. | | `lsm` | `0.0` | Larval source management coverage from the campaign. | The first four are the current net mix, whose coverages are summed to give `itn_use` and whose `dn0` values are averaged to give `dn0_use`. The rest describe the campaign. `routine` and `lsm` carry no `_future` suffix but belong to the campaign all the same. Like `dn0_future`, `itn_future` and `irs_future`, they are held at zero for every timestep before day 3285, and take their supplied value only from the campaign onwards. ::: {.callout-important} ## Future coverage must be set explicitly If `itn_future` is 0 or `net_type_future` is `None`, then `dn0_future` and `itn_future` are both set to 0 and the nets are **withdrawn** at the campaign. `irs_future` behaves the same way and does not inherit from `irs`. To hold an intervention steady you have to restate it. A setting with pyrethroid-only nets at 0.70 coverage that keeps them needs `itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only"` written out in full. Omit it and the nets have been modelled as abandoned, and the rebound in the trajectory is then real output from a scenario nobody intended. ::: ## Five scenarios The five scenarios below vary every axis the pipeline exposes. They use all three input modes, all four net products and none, both seasonality settings, IRS and larval source management, and a mosquito-density adjustment in both directions. They are not five options competing with one another, and there is no shared baseline. Each is a different way of driving the API. ::: {#bf9dee3a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import run_scenarios from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget grid = [ # A prevalence survey, pyrethroid-only nets held at their current coverage. Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only, prevalence", res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), py_only=0.70, itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only"), # A seasonal setting under PBO nets and IRS, with mosquito density rising 60%. Scenario(name="PBO, +60% mosquitoes", res_use=0.55, Q0=0.90, phi=0.85, seasonal=1.0, irs=0.40, eir_target=EirTarget(0.30, "prevalence"), py_pbo=0.85, mosquito_delta=0.60, itn_future=0.85, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.40), # Pyrrole nets plus larviciding, with mosquito density halved. Scenario(name="Pyrrole + LSM, -50% mosquitoes", res_use=0.70, Q0=0.75, phi=0.70, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.30, "prevalence"), py_pyrrole=0.60, mosquito_delta=-0.50, itn_future=0.60, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", lsm=0.30), # Entomological evidence instead of a survey. The biting rate is inverted, not a prevalence. Scenario(name="PPF, biting rate", res_use=0.45, Q0=0.80, phi=0.82, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(250_000.0, "hbr"), py_ppf=0.50, itn_future=0.50, net_type_future="pyrethroid_ppf"), # The EIR is already known, so estiMINT does nothing. IRS only, no nets at all. Scenario(name="No nets, EIR given", res_use=0.0, Q0=0.88, phi=0.78, seasonal=1.0, irs=0.60, eir_target=EirTarget(20.0, "eir"), irs_future=0.60), ] res = run_scenarios(grid) res.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (5, 23) ``` ::: ::: One call runs all five. `run_scenarios` derives `dn0` from each net mix, inverts each `eir_target` according to its mode, and applies any mosquito-density adjustment. It then assembles the twelve covariates and calls the emulator once with the whole batch. Five rows and twenty-three columns come back. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Net type names `net_type_future` accepts `"pyrethroid_pbo"` or the short alias `"py_pbo"`. It does not accept `"pyrethroid-pbo"`. A hyphen raises `ValueError: unknown net type`. ::: ## The returned columns The columns fall into four groups. The first is what you asked for, resolved, which reduces the current net mix to a single product name and reports the mode each scenario ran in. ::: {#2325a3f4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["name", "input_mode", "net", "net_future"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name input_mode net net_future
0 Pyrethroid-only, prevalence prevalence py_only pyrethroid_only
1 PBO, +60% mosquitoes prevalence py_pbo pyrethroid_pbo
2 Pyrrole + LSM, -50% mosquitoes prevalence py_pyrrole pyrethroid_pyrrole
3 PPF, biting rate hbr py_ppf pyrethroid_ppf
4 No nets, EIR given eir none none
``` ::: ::: All three input modes appear in `input_mode`. With no campaign nets, `net_future` comes back as the string `"none"` rather than as a missing value, which is what the final row shows. The second group is the covariates the emulator actually saw. These are derived rather than echoed, so reading them back is how you check that the scenario which ran is the one you built. ::: {#19647139 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[[ "dn0_use", "itn_use", "irs_use", "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future", "routine", "lsm", "seasonal", ]].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
dn0_use itn_use irs_use dn0_future itn_future irs_future routine lsm seasonal
0 0.3110 0.70 0.0 0.3110 0.70 0.0 0.0 0.000 0.0
1 0.4456 0.85 0.4 0.4456 0.85 0.4 0.0 0.000 1.0
2 0.5082 0.60 0.0 0.5082 0.60 0.0 0.0 0.300 0.0
3 0.3828 0.50 0.0 0.3828 0.50 0.0 0.0 0.124 0.0
4 0.0000 0.00 0.6 0.0000 0.00 0.6 0.0 0.000 1.0
``` ::: ::: `dn0_use` is the usage-weighted `dn0` of the current mix, and `itn_use` the sum of its coverages. `dn0_future` is the `dn0` of the campaign product at the same resistance. Note that `lsm` is not always the `lsm` you passed. `run_scenarios` folds PPF net coverage into effective larval source management before the emulator runs, under the rule set out in [Pipeline architecture](../07-under-the-hood/architecture.qmd). The fourth row passed no `lsm` at all and comes back with one. The third group is transmission intensity. `eir_baseline` is what the inversion produced, `eir_final` is that EIR after `mosquito_delta` has been applied, and the two are equal whenever the delta is zero. ::: {#1cfcb155 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["input_mode", "eir_baseline", "mosquito_delta", "eir_final", "hbr_baseline", "hbr_new"]].round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
input_mode eir_baseline mosquito_delta eir_final hbr_baseline hbr_new
0 prevalence 32.0 0.0 32.0 NaN NaN
1 prevalence 106.7 0.6 204.2 880248.3 1408397.3
2 prevalence 15.0 -0.5 6.9 275318.3 137659.1
3 hbr 12.5 0.0 12.5 NaN NaN
4 eir 20.0 0.0 20.0 NaN NaN
``` ::: ::: The last row shows the `"eir"` mode passing 20 straight through untouched. In the second row a 60% rise in mosquito density roughly doubles the EIR. In the third, halving the density cuts the EIR by more than half. Neither response is proportional to the change that produced it. `hbr_baseline` and `hbr_new` are populated only for those two rows. The HBR is an intermediate in the mosquito-density calculation and is not otherwise computed, so everywhere else it is `NaN`. The fourth group is outcomes. `prev_y9` is prevalence at the campaign. For a scenario that supplied a prevalence it should come back close to what was supplied, and the small gap is the round trip through the inversion and the emulator. ::: {#46f35c5a .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["name", "prev_y9", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"]].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
name prev_y9 prev_endline cases_endline
0 Pyrethroid-only, prevalence 0.4560 0.4837 2.4331
1 PBO, +60% mosquitoes 0.2611 0.2912 0.3279
2 Pyrrole + LSM, -50% mosquitoes 0.1979 0.1624 1.0566
3 PPF, biting rate 0.3049 0.2972 1.6823
4 No nets, EIR given 0.0062 0.0089 0.0358
``` ::: ::: The first row supplied 0.45 and recovers 0.456. The second and third both supplied 0.30, and recover 0.261 and 0.198. Note that the third is well off, and deliberately so. A mosquito-density adjustment of −50% moves the EIR away from the one that sustained the measured prevalence, which is the whole point of supplying it. `prev_endline` and `cases_endline` are the last window of the horizon, three years on. ## The trajectories The last two columns, `prevalence` and `cases`, are not scalars. Each cell holds the full trajectory as a 157-element NumPy array, stored inside the DataFrame rather than unrolled into a tidy long table. ::: {#db777585 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} prev = np.asarray(res.loc[0, "prevalence"]) type(prev), prev.shape, prev.dtype ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` (numpy.ndarray, (157,), dtype('float32')) ``` ::: ::: This is convenient for a five-row grid and awkward for anything else. The frame cannot be written to CSV as it stands, and any comparison across scenarios has to reach into the cells first. [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) deals with both. The 157 windows are a property of the emulator, so read the grid off the artefact rather than hard-coding it. `preload_models` returns the three `estimint` XGBoost models and the two `stateMINT` artefacts, which are the same objects `run_scenarios` uses internally. Calling it once up front also warms the caches and pulls the weights from Hugging Face before the first run rather than during it. ::: {#9f2e0b94 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import preload_models xgb_models, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] window = cfg["window_size"] start = cfg["model_start_day"] campaign = cfg["intervention_day"] abs_t = start + window * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - campaign) / 365 idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - campaign))) n_steps, window, start, campaign, idx_y9 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` (157, 14, 2190, 3285, 78) ``` ::: ::: `idx_y9` is the index of the window the campaign falls in. Everything before it is baseline and everything from it onwards is response, and in `years` the campaign sits at zero. ::: {#04b24731 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} float(years[0]), float(years[idx_y9]), float(years[-1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` (-3.0, -0.00821917808219178, 2.9835616438356163) ``` ::: ::: The horizon covers three years of baseline and three years of response. A trajectory can then be taken out of a cell and plotted against that axis in two lines. ::: {#d12c2439 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.8)) for _, row in res.iterrows(): ax.plot(years, np.asarray(row["prevalence"]), lw=1.8, label=row["name"]) ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_xlabel("Years since campaign") ax.set_ylabel("Prevalence (under 5)") ax.set_ylim(0, None) ax.legend(fontsize=7.5) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Prevalence under all five scenarios. The dashed line marks the campaign at year 0, and everything to its left is the run-up under whatever was already in place.](run-scenarios_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of under-five prevalence for five scenarios from three years before the campaign to three years after. The scenarios start at different levels because each describes a different setting, and each responds differently to its own campaign. The EIR-input scenario sits near zero throughout.'} ::: ::: The five lines start at different levels. Unlike a grid, these scenarios describe five different settings rather than five campaigns in one, so there is no shared baseline to converge on. The three years to the left of the dashed line are each model's run-up to its campaign, under whatever was already in place. The prevalence you supply is therefore prevalence at the campaign, not at the start of the horizon. The value to check it against is `prev_y9`. ## The weights repository Both `run_scenarios` and `preload_models` take an `hf_repo` argument, defaulting to `"dide-ic/stateMINT"`. ```python res = run_scenarios(grid, hf_repo="dide-ic/stateMINT") ``` Change it to run against a fork or a local snapshot of the weights. Note that `run_scenarios` tracks whatever `main` currently points at in that repository, and exposes no revision pin. If an analysis has to be reproducible years from now, either record the weight version alongside the results, or drive the emulator directly with a pinned `revision` as in [Calling the emulator](../05-statemint/the-emulator.qmd). ## See also [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd) builds five campaigns against one shared baseline rather than five separate settings, and [Trajectories and cases](comparing.qmd) plots and integrates what comes back. What the emulator sees once a scenario has been resolved is set out in [Covariates and the time grid](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd). Please see [Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) for where `dn0_use` and `dn0_future` come from.
